procedural_history.originating_court: Sessions Court, Bengaluru (Principal City Civil and Sessions Judge)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 28.04.2017 passed by the High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru in Crl. Petition No. 2351 of 2017, recalling its own order dated 18.04.2017.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant approached the High Court, aggrieved by a notice issued by the Sessions Court on 25.01.2017 in Criminal Appeal No. 95/2017. The High Court initially passed an order on 18.04.2017. Subsequently, the High Court passed an order on 28.04.2017 recalling its earlier order of 18.04.2017, stating that the earlier order was patently erroneous.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant, aggrieved by the High Court's order dated 28.04.2017 recalling its earlier order, approached the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court held that the High Court should not have exercised the power under Section 362 Cr.P.C. to recall its order for a correction on merits. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order dated 28.04.2017 and directed the Principal City Civil and Sessions Judge, Bengaluru, to dispose of Criminal Appeal No. 95/2017 expeditiously. The Supreme Court also set aside the order dated 18.04.2017 passed by the High Court.

directions: The impugned order dated 28.04.2017 is set aside.
The order dated 18.04.2017 passed by the High Court is set aside.
The Principal City Civil and Sessions Judge, Bengalure is directed to dispose of the Criminal Appeal No.95/2017 expeditiously.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court has the power under Section 362 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, to recall its own order on the merits, on the ground that the order was patently erroneous.

facts: The High Court passed an order on 18.04.2017.
Subsequently, on 28.04.2017, the High Court recalled its own order, stating that the earlier order was "patently erroneous."
The Supreme Court reviewed the propriety of this recall order.
law: Section 362 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (Cr.P.C.) allows a court to correct only clerical or arithmetical errors in its judgments or final orders.
This section does not permit a court to review or alter its own order on the merits of the case.
application: The Supreme Court observed that the High Court did not correct a clerical or arithmetical error.
Instead, the High Court sought to "re-hear the matter on merits" because it believed its previous decision was wrong.
The Court held that this action goes beyond the limited scope of Section 362 Cr.P.C.
It emphasized that even if an order is "patently erroneous," it must be corrected through a proper legal process (like an appeal), not by the same court recalling it under Section 362.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court's action was impermissible under law. It held that a High Court does not have the power under Section 362 Cr.P.C. to recall its own order on the merits, regardless of how erroneous that order might be.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court has the power under Section 362 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, to recall its own order on the merits, on the ground that the order was patently erroneous.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the High Court erred in passing an order under Section 362 Cr.P.C. to recall its own previous order on the merits. The appellant's contention was that this action was impermissible under law.
respondent_arguments: The provided text does not explicitly state the arguments made by the respondents.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The power under Section 362 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is strictly limited to correcting a clerical or arithmetical error and cannot be used to review or correct a judgment on its merits, regardless of how patently erroneous the earlier order may be.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The power of a High Court under Section 362 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is strictly limited to the correction of a clerical or arithmetical error. It cannot be exercised to correct an order on its merits, regardless of how patently erroneous that earlier order may be. An attempt to re-hear a matter on the merits because the previous order was erroneous is impermissible under this section.
legal_tests_applied: The court applied a test to determine the scope of Section 362 Cr.P.C., distinguishing between a 'clerical or arithmetical error' and a 'correction on merits'. The power is only available for the former.
why_respondent_won: The appellant's argument was accepted by the court. The High Court's action of recalling its own order on the ground that it was 'patently erroneous' was found to be an impermissible re-hearing of the matter on the merits.
The court held that the whole purpose of Section 362 Cr.P.C. is only to correct a clerical or arithmetical error, and what the High Court sought to do did not fall into this category.
The court reasoned that even a patently erroneous order can only be corrected through the proper 'process known to law' (such as an appeal), not by invoking Section 362 Cr.P.C.
